review: I don't even know why I like the Faerie Solitaire games, but I do.

Faerie Solitaire Harvest, developed by Subsoap and published on Steam by Puppygames, takes the deceptively simple framework of match-two solitaire and transforms it into a layered fantasy adventure built around progression, collection, and gentle strategic depth. At first glance, it presents itself as a cozy card game wrapped in bright colors and soft magical aesthetics, but the longer you spend with it, the clearer it becomes that the design is driven by a careful balance between accessibility and long-term engagement. Rather than relying solely on the inherent appeal of solitaire mechanics, the game builds an interconnected system of exploration, pet evolution, resource management, and board mastery that steadily unfolds across dozens of handcrafted stages.

The core gameplay revolves around pairing cards of equal value to clear them from the board, a mechanic that is immediately intuitive even to players unfamiliar with more complex solitaire variants. However, Faerie Solitaire Harvest quickly adds nuance through layered board layouts, combo systems, and limited move efficiency. Each stage presents a distinct arrangement of cards, some straightforward and others deliberately intricate, requiring thoughtful sequencing rather than random matching. Because cards are often stacked or gated behind others, players must consider the consequences of each pair cleared. A careless match can block access to more efficient chains, while a carefully planned sequence can cascade into satisfying multi-clear combos that dramatically shift the board state.

Progression is fueled by the accumulation of resources such as Pure Gold and mana, which tie the card mechanics into the broader adventure structure. Winning efficiently and building longer chains generates greater rewards, encouraging players to replay stages for improved performance. The resource system avoids feeling grindy because it is directly tied to skillful play; the better you manage the board, the more quickly you progress. This creates a loop that feels both relaxing and quietly competitive, as players often find themselves attempting to optimize earlier levels to maximize returns.

One of the most distinctive elements of the game is its magical pet system. As you advance through the faerie world, you hatch and raise collectible creatures that evolve over time. These pets are more than cosmetic additions; they represent milestones in progression and provide narrative flavor to the experience. Each evolution feels like a small reward for consistent play, adding emotional investment to what could otherwise be a purely abstract card game. The act of nurturing and completing collections adds a subtle RPG-like layer, giving players long-term goals beyond simply clearing boards. This collectible system also strengthens the sense of worldbuilding, making the Faerie realm feel inhabited and alive rather than just a backdrop for puzzles.

Visually, the game leans into a bright, hand-painted fantasy style that reinforces its cozy tone. Each location is rendered with vibrant colors and whimsical environmental details, from enchanted forests to mystical ruins. While the gameplay itself unfolds primarily on card layouts, the surrounding art provides context and atmosphere that elevate the experience. The presentation is polished without being overwhelming, and the interface remains clean and readable even as boards become more complex. Animations are smooth and unobtrusive, complementing the relaxed pace rather than distracting from it.

The pacing of Faerie Solitaire Harvest is deliberately measured. It is not a game built for rapid-fire sessions or adrenaline-driven play. Instead, it thrives on a calm rhythm of observation, planning, and gradual accumulation of rewards. This slower tempo will appeal strongly to players who enjoy thoughtful puzzle-solving and incremental progression. At the same time, later stages introduce greater board complexity, forcing players to think several moves ahead. While the early game is forgiving and welcoming, the difficulty curve ensures that mastery requires patience and strategic awareness.

Replayability is supported through multiple modes, including options to revisit stages for improved scores and additional challenges. Because each board is handcrafted rather than procedurally generated, the layouts feel intentionally designed, often hiding clever card placements that reward experimentation. Completionists will find satisfaction in fully evolving pets, unlocking all locations, and earning achievements tied to efficient clears. The New Game Plus option adds further longevity, allowing players to experience the adventure with heightened stakes and refined strategy.

Despite its strengths, the game’s appeal is closely tied to appreciation of its genre. Players seeking dramatic narrative twists or mechanically complex systems may find the structure repetitive over long stretches. The core loop remains focused on card matching, and while progression systems add variety, they do not fundamentally alter the gameplay formula. However, for those who enjoy structured puzzle progression and collection-based motivation, this consistency becomes a virtue rather than a flaw.

Ultimately, Faerie Solitaire Harvest succeeds because it understands how to expand a simple concept without overcomplicating it. It blends solitaire mechanics with fantasy worldbuilding, pet evolution, and resource-driven progression in a way that feels cohesive and inviting. The result is a relaxing yet strategically engaging experience that rewards patience, observation, and incremental mastery. For players who appreciate cozy puzzle games with meaningful long-term goals and charming presentation, it offers a polished and content-rich journey through a magical world built on the quiet satisfaction of matching cards and watching something grow.

I was quite a fan of the original Faerie Solitaire and I'm even more of a fan of the remastered version, so I expected to enjoy this one too. There I was wrong.

The basic premise is that of matching identical pairs of cards to clear the board. Like Faerie Solitaire, the cards are various mythical creatures, and these ones are more detailed and also some of them quite scary looking as befits magical beings! You get extra points through matching identical cards e.g. Red Aces although you can also clear the board by matching the values but not the colour e.g. Red and Black Queen.

Unlike the original Faerie Solitaire there seems to be very little story and there is also very little variation. Thus the game swiftly becomes repetitive. Also, like the original version of Faerie Solitaire you do collect pets and then resources to evolve these pets (sound familiar, Nintendo?) but the process of collecting and evolving is incredibly slow (something the remastered version of Faerie solitaire corrects). You also collect some gemstones which are called 'Lore' - presumably these are meant to flesh out the 'world' as you read little excerpts by clicking on them. Frankly, I thought this was all so boring that there wasn't any point - it could have been vastly improved if they had helped you unlock special abilities etc.

All in all this game very quickly gets repetitive and without things to help you with the game play (the original had 'undo' and 'see next card' functions, and I can't see how the complicated system of 'valor' etc. helps with anything here) it swiftly becomes a grind.

Personally, I wouldn't bother with this one unless you are just planning to play it for a 10 minute session in-between other things as perhaps then it won't seem too much of a slog. I would just buy the remastered original.

Recommended, but with some significant caveats.

If you liked the original game, you'll feel at home with this one.
However- the interesting features such as locked cards and vines are gone, replaced by new (often frustrating) layouts, Skill Trees, and Valors- ways to make the game more difficult with a "Valor" level that has to be leveled up to unlock. Valors are supposed to bring greater rewards with them, but the benefits seemed far outweighed by the sometimes significant limitations some of the Valors place on the player, leading to replaying some hands more than just a few times to pass them.

No story as you play, like the original. Instead you unlock "Lore" that tells the story, often in an overdone and a bit too overblown of a way (at least in the English language version). 

NG+ levels are more difficult and contain more complex layouts, some of which are extremely difficult to pass even without any Valors applied, requiring a good bit of luck to get a good deal, and a good number of wild cards to get through.

Valors can be changed at any time, but the changes only go into effect at the start of a new level, and last for the entire level, even if you deactivate the Valor midway through.

The art is pretty, pretty much the same as the Faerie Solitaire Remastered version of the game. 
The music is fine, but repetitive.
Drop rates for resources are pretty skimpy, especially considering the amount needed to evolve some of the pets, especially the higher tiers.

It's a fine solitaire game, but far too much grind to make getting to NG+3 fun. Just grindy. 
Games that take a long time to complete =/= "good".

Others have done it in less (maybe without Valors applied?), others have taken much longer.

Still, too grindy for my liking, with little reason to play once you unlock all of the Lore story bits, other than completing all achievements. Buy on sale, and expect to grind for a long time.

[h1]Není solitaire jako solitaire[/h1]
A začnu hned tím, co je největším záporem tohohle titulu. Není to solitaire. Respektive herní mechanika je zcela jiná, než jaká byla v prvním díle, který se mi hodně líbil. Právě na základě toho jsem si koupil i dvojku a nestačil se divit, co za móresy se tu děje. Zatímco dříve jste na sebe skládali karty tak, jak jdou dle hodnoty (ať už vzestupně nebo sestupně), zde je to prakticky spoj 2. Nebo takové těžší pexeso. Nebo pokud jste trošku zkušenější na poli karetních her, tak se jedná o mahjong solitaire. Na herní ploše máte rozmístěné kartičky a když najdete druhou stejnou, tak zmizí z herní plochy. Úkolem je samozřejmě ji zcela vyčistit. Máte tu i balíček, ze kterého si vybíráte karty, pak místo na odložení jedné karty a samozřejmě žolíky (získáváte je díky kombům).

Bohužel to je tak vše, co se týče herních mechanik. Zapomeňte na nějaké speciální druhy karet a na jakékoliv překážky (zámky, řetězy, oheň apod.), které musíte nejprve sejmout z karet, abyste je poté mohli označit. Čeká tu na vás čtyřicítka levelů, která se ale vůbec ničím neliší (maximálně tak barvou pozadí a tím, že každá další úroveň je o ždibínek těžší).

[h1]Zahraj to znovu, Same[/h1]
Bohužel, zde negativa nekončí. Příběh je vyprávěn skrze nalezené střípky informací, takže ve zkratce – vůbec tu není. Zároveň tu naleznete i vajíčka, která musíte vyvinout v dospělé tvory. Něco podobného bylo už v prvním díle. Jenže věcí, které potřebujete na jejich vývin, tu je strašně málo a co je dle mě ještě horší je fakt, že hra počítá s tím, že si ji sjedete několikrát po sobě. Takže po dokončení posledního levelu se vám celá hra přehodí na New Game + a vy si můžete hrát levely až do aleluja s pár bonusy (padá víc materiálu). Netuším, kolik času se potřebuje na tenhle grind, abyste měli vše, ale už jenom ta představa, že 40 stěží rozeznatelných a prakticky stejných levelů opakujete furt a pořád dokola, je otřesná. Ano, grind vajíček a těch tvorů byl už v prvním díle, ale tady to šlo vyřešit elegantněji (buď snížit počet tvorů, zrychlit jejich růst, případně zvětšit příjem surovin, dát tam víc levelů nebo u levelů v NG+ přidat nějaké nové herní mechaniky…).

[h1]Dohráno jednou, dohráno napořád[/h1]
Hra má i několik dobrých věcí. Pokud se přenesete přes onu herní mechaniku a repetitivnost levelů a nutnost hrát celou hru opět od začátku, tak vás jistě potěší možnost investovat získané peníze do nejrůznějších vymožeností. Ano, je tu strom schopností a je dost velký. Některé bonusy mi přišly nic moc, prakticky od začátku jsem všechny peníze cpal do zvětšení příjmů, abych si mohl odemknout ještě více schopností. Jenže většina z nich nestojí pouze peníze, ale také víly, které zachraňujete. To znamená 40 při jednom průchodu celou kampaní. Asi už chápete, kam tím směřuju. Je to nedostatek a víl musíte zachránit o DOST víc, abyste si odemkli všechny ty schopnosti. Také je můžete resetovat a dokonce dostanete i část peněz nazpět.

I got the chance to compare 'harvest' to the first installment and I feel like the gameplay compares negatively.

I liked the original Faerie Solitaire better.  But this is more challenging, card matching instead of in series, and still has the pets.

Good news is every time you level or finish a map section, you get a talent point to spend.  Bad news is you need at least 10,000 "Pure" to buy a talent once you have enough points and as much as 50,000 Pure.  Good news is you earn Pure with every card match.  Bad news is if you are unable to finish a hand, you must spend 1,000 Pure to retry.  You have no other option.  None.  You cannot re-deal or opt out of the hand.  You're forced to spend your Pure.

This makes the game incredibly tedious.  You only need one bad hand to wipe our your gold and put those bonus and power-ups your talents are suppose to enable out of reach.  This makes the game wildly imbalanced.  Since the card deals are a matter of RNG (or luck if you prefer), there's no skill involved that makes the game less punishing.   

The game play has nothing particular to recommend it.  It's a match solitaire on a plain board with very little visual interest.  The non-traditional cards are difficult to sort out because many of the images on the cards are nearly the same in design and color. 

There are pets, but there is no indication that they do anything to assist you, nor do the faeries you release.  They are just there to give you a little carrot, should collecting pets and faeries be your thing.  

I don't recommend this game for its repetitive, uninteresting gameplay, and the punishing design of its redeals and talent system.

The extras (bonuses, talents) are simple "ooh shiny" moments. They add a self-challenging mode (how can I improve my own efficiency to get higher points  / evolve pets / whatever) which is enjoyable because it's not forced. There is also a higher difficulty mode which is satisfying both from gameplay and the "ooh shiny" rewards. I was not a fan of the forced and cheesy "story" in the original so this map-based system suits my style of play just fine.,

This game works perfectly on my Windows Surface 2 Pro in tablet mode, which is a great bonus for goofing off while watching something "meh" on TV.

I do wish they had additional deck designs (workshop, achievement, or a cheap purpose) as the card backs are a little ... odd.

I recommend this as a fun, casual, and just-enough-stimulating brain game.

If it ain't broken, don't fix it - says the proverb. Case of Faerie Solitaire Harvest is the case of "fixing" very nice and relaxing predecessor, making it somehow worse. I have almost 60 hours in previous installment, but this one is just simply not fun.  

Dropping the previous set of rules, where you matched cards one up or down, regardless of suit, to match two - is main fun killer. As result the gameplay is much more random, killing enjoyment out of doing huge combos and breaking the quite dynamic game flow. Forced repeating of failed stage also adds insult to injury. I did first stage like 6 times. C'mon, that's not a good experience for new players, even in regular title, not mention casual one like this.

Taking out the story wasn't a nice thing for me too. While it wasn't complex and serious, it added reason for stage changes and offered some art. This one really felt like lack of effort.

And since match two is core rule, Faerie Solitaire Harvest is sadly unfixable and I will refund it. I also won't recommend it even for people who didn't play it's predecessor, as very random nature and forced stage repeating, makes it quite an frustrating experience. And this isn't what I look in relaxing game.

If you don't want to read the full review, my opinion is that yes, this game is absolutely worth $10. A fun, relaxing match-two solitaire game with some serious depth for hardcore gamers to dive into. Can really be as chilled out and casual or as "hardcore" as you want it to be, and some recent updates (while I've been playing through the game) have seriously improved the game a lot. If you want to try it out for a bit before buying, a "free" version on the winrar model (will ask you to buy every so often) can be played in-browser here: https://www.solitaire.io/

Full description/review:

Okay to start, each "hand" starts you with cards in a pre-arranged pattern on the board, with a deck from which you can draw cards to assist you. the goal is to clear the board of cards, although a recent update now allows you to progress without getting it 100% clear. Match two cards of the same number to clear them, and if they're also the same color it will start a combo. Getting a combo of at least 7 cards will allow you to redeal the deck for free, although higher combos will allow you to earn more of the in-game currency. Wild cards are earned while playing by accumulating mana, and can be used to match with a card to remove it, although this can be a trap as it will leave a same numbered card somewhere on the board or in the deck without a pair. While playing, you will also see various other items "drop": "lore shards" which give a snippet of story about the world, "eggs" which can be hatched into pets, and "crafting materials" which are used to "evolve" said pets.

The game's primary currency, Pure, is gained while matching cards as well as based on bonuses at the end of a hand: your highest combo reached being a major one, plus ones for things like clearing the board without using the deck, one for clearing all of the the deck, foundations, and board, and a few others. In addition, you will gain talent points while playing, one for clearing a location (set of 9 hands) as well as one for each level gained in valor (more on that later.) These two combined can be used to purchase "talents" (skills) that give you benefits while playing: making it easier to combo, increased drop rates, various tactical advantages, and more. This system adds a significant amount of depth and customization to the game.

In addition to talents, the other main system that adds depth to the game is its "valor" system, optional conducts which are unlocked through various accomplishments in-game and can be activated to provide additional challenge in exchange for more rapid gain of valor levels (and thus more talent points.) examples include no wilds, a halved deck size, and being unable to use the spare space on the board. the more of these conducts active the higher the valor xp gain, but beware: with any valor conducts active you must now clear the entire board in order to progress to the next hand as well as fulfilling the conditions for whatever valors you have activated. if you wish to change your active valors, you must restart the entire 9-hand location!
Overall, I found this game incredibly deep with a clear sense of progression across my ~100 hours played through three loops of the game (i have inadvertantly left the game running while asleep a couple times so my time played is a bit off hehe) I enjoyed this game quite a lot, and despite being constantly dragged by my so-called friends for playing it all the time I don't regret my time with it or money spent in any way. Strong recommend!

I have to give this games a thumbs up, everything works, and the bits and pieces are nice, but it really seems to miss the mark. This could have been a good 7 or 8 out of 10, rather than the 5 that it is. 
The core game is a card matching game. Cards are laid out in a wide patterns, overlapping, and only the top cards can be picked. 
The scoring is made up of gold, and valor, which can be used to purchase upgrades and abilities that in turn open the game up, giving you more tactical and strategic options.
Built in is the motivation of match colors (hearts and diamonds are both red, etc. just like a regular deck of cards) and after you've played awhile you realize the value of at least getting seven in a row at the start, in order to get a second run thru the deck for free.
As you progress, you earn Wild Magic, which in turn generates wild cards, which, as you might imagine, can match with any card.
Your goal is to clear all the cards from the board, though doing so while using all of the cards in the hand at well generates a nice bonus.
Here is an odd bump in the road, and it makes me wonder about the developers.
Other reviews will show that the need to pay for the second run thru the deck has upset a lot of people. I have never had a problem getting the minimum seven in a row, but I do often have to go pretty deep into the deck to do this, I suspect this concerns some players.
The incredibly obvious fix is to allow people to simply quit out if they reach the end of the first run thru the deck without earning the second run thru free, but they haven't done this. Very confusing. Cannot imagine why.
Anyway, as you play the game, you unlock really interesting lore, pet eggs, and resources useful for various things. 
It sounds like a perfect package, except most of it doesn't mean anything.
The lore tells a fascinating story, but is as disconnected from the game as if you were playing solitaire while reading a book. 
Even more frustrating is the eggs, which eventually hatch into pets, then evolve into cool forms, that do absolutely nothing.
There have been hints and rumors that this might change, but they are always couched very carefully in such a way as to promise nothing.
Another odd disconnect, like the previously mentioned bump in the road. The game has a wide selection of talents you can buy, why were the pets not hooked into these? They already exist. It seems quite a simple step to have the pets help open the talents.
Without a purpose, why would anyone go back and replay old levels to earn resources, when the main reason for resources is to activate the pets? 
And on top of all that, you are freeing fairies, one for each set of nine areas, and they are also meaningless, bland muguffins. 
So after all this griping, why a thumbs up? Because the game works, the music nice, and the controls work pretty well ninety percent of the time. It is fun, in fact if there was less here, I would probably be more pleased with it. An odd place for a game to come to.
One last gripe though...
One of the talents I have invested in turns some of the under-cards face up. The problem is, you can't always tell which color that under-card is. Unlike real playing cards, the suit is only identified int he top left corner, and not the bottom left. Again, it seems a simple fix, really adding a red or black border around the edge of the card or image would suffice, there seems to be no interest from the developers to make this little fix. If they ignore such simple fixes as this, and the ability to quit out, forcing you to spend your resources on a second run thru the deck, it is hard to expect them to actually be working on the bigger aspects of the game.
Still, if it's on sale, it's fun, and that's enough to give it a thumbs up.

Edit : On Reddit saw some comments about how hard it is to advance, sometimes you just can't win a deal. That's baloney. My very simple strategy is to match all NON-COLOR-MATCHED pairs, then deal 3 cards. Match all color-matched pairs, deal until you make a 7-match combo, then keep going as normal. Use your free space and wilds. I haven't lost a round since I started this, probably 15 games won in a row.

Edit 2 : Much farther into the game. Now the progression gate is Talent Points. You get one each time you beat all levels in a world. It's easy to earn a lot of PureGold, but hard to spend it because of the dearth of talent points.
